nameStory: This lichen gets its 'smokey-eyed' name from its distinctive dark-rimmed fruiting bodies that look like tiny eyes with dark, sooty eyeliner. The 'boulder' part is straightforward – you'll almost always find this crusty lichen growing directly on large rocks and boulders, where it forms tight patches.
description: Smokey-eyed Boulder Lichen is a crusty, paint-like lichen that grows in thin patches directly on rock surfaces. It forms grayish to bluish-gray crusts that can spread several inches across, looking almost like someone dabbed rough paint onto the stone. The most noticeable features are its small, dark-rimmed circular discs (called apothecia) that dot the crusty surface like tiny dark eyes.

idTips.label: Dark-rimmed fruiting discs
idTips.description: Look for small, round, dark discs with prominent black rims scattered across the lichen surface – these look remarkably like tiny smokey eyes and feel slightly raised when you run your finger over them

idTips.label: Crusty rock-hugging growth
idTips.description: Forms thin, paint-like crusts that adhere tightly to rock – you can't peel this lichen off like you might with leafy lichens, and it feels rough and gritty to the touch

idTips.label: Bluish-gray coloration
idTips.description: The main body has a distinctive grayish to pale bluish-gray color that often looks slightly chalky or powdery, especially when dry

idTips.label: Rock substrate preference
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found growing on hard rock surfaces, particularly granite and other acidic stones – rarely seen on bark, soil, or softer substrates

idTips.label: Patch size and texture
idTips.description: Forms irregular patches typically 2-6 inches across with a rough, granular texture that feels like fine sandpaper when touched gently

habitat: Look for Smokey-eyed Boulder Lichen on exposed granite outcrops, large boulders, and rock faces throughout New England's mountains and rocky areas. It particularly favors acidic rocks in partially shaded to fully exposed locations, from sea-level rocky shores up to mountain summits. You'll often find it sharing rock surfaces with other crusty lichens and mosses in areas with good air circulation.

seasonality.spring: The dark-rimmed fruiting discs become more prominent as humidity increases, making identification easier. Spring rains bring out the bluish-gray coloration more vividly.
seasonality.summer: During dry periods, the lichen may appear more grayish and chalky, but the diagnostic dark-rimmed discs remain visible. Best viewing is after summer rainstorms when colors are refreshed.
seasonality.fall: Increased moisture makes the lichen more vibrant and easier to spot against autumn-colored surroundings. The contrast between the smokey discs and lighter body is most pronounced.
seasonality.winter: Still visible and identifiable on snow-free rock surfaces, though colors may appear more muted. The dark fruiting discs stand out well against snow-covered rocks.

funFact: This lichen can actually help geologists estimate the age of rock surfaces – some crusty boulder lichens grow incredibly slowly, expanding only millimeters per year, so a dinner-plate-sized patch might be decades or even centuries old!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other crusty rock lichens, but the distinctive dark-rimmed "smokey eyes" are the key – if you see those prominent black-rimmed circular discs, you've likely found your smokey-eyed friend rather than a plain gray crusty lichen.
contextualKnowledge: Like many lichens, this species is actually two organisms living together – a fungus and an algae in partnership. The scientific name 'albocaerulescens' means 'white-bluish,' referring to its characteristic coloration that can shift between whitish and bluish tones.
compareHints: Unlike the Concentric Boulder Lichen which has target-like rings in its fruiting discs, Smokey-eyed Boulder Lichen has simple dark-rimmed circles. Big-disk Pebble Lichen has much larger fruiting bodies, while Orange Boulder Lichen is distinctly orange-tinted rather than bluish-gray. The smokey-eyed species is unique in having that perfect combination of bluish-gray color and prominent dark eye-like rims.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Concentric boulder lichen stands out from its Porpidia relatives by its distinctive ring patterns - Smokey-eyed Boulder Lichen lacks these concentric circles and appears more uniformly colored, while Orange Boulder Lichen has obvious orange tints that make it unmistakable.
Among its Porpidia relatives, big-disk pebble lichen stands out for having the largest and most prominent apothecia - the 'macrocarpa' in its scientific name literally means 'large fruit.
Orange Boulder Lichen stands out from its Porpidia relatives by its brilliant orange color, while Smokey-eyed Boulder Lichen is more gray-blue and Concentric Boulder Lichen forms circular patterns.
